title.en: The Forging of Mjollnir: Loki, the Fly and the Dwarf-Brothers
title.zh: 妙爾尼爾的鍛造：洛基、蒼蠅與矮人兄弟

region.en: The dwarf forges under the earth (symbolic pin at Pingvellir, Iceland)
region.zh: 地下的矮人鍛爐（象徵性定位於冰島辛格韋德利）

texts.period: Skaldskaparmal c. 1220-1230 (older mythic material); principal MSS Codex Regius GKS 2367 4to, Codex Trajectinus

source.work: Snorri, Skaldskaparmal ch. 2-3 (the treasures of the gods); critical ed. Faulkes (1987)

texts.license: Public domain (Brodeur 1916); passages below are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: To replace the hair Loki cut from Sif, the dwarf sons of Ivaldi forge golden hair, the ring Draupnir and the ship Skidbladnir; Loki then bets his head that the brothers Brokkr and Eitri cannot forge better. At their forge a fly - Loki in disguise - stings the smith's hands and neck to spoil the work; on the third attempt the fly stings the eyelid, blood runs, and Eitri draws out the hammer Mjollnir with a short handle. At the judgment the gods rule that the hammer is best of all - it can be small in the shirt, it never misses, it returns to the hand - and the dwarf moves to behead Loki, whose neck (no part of the head) is saved by a deus ex stitch: the gods cut the holes to enlarge the neck. The record is the aition of the god of thunder's signature weapon and of the dwarf-gift economy.
summary.zh: 為補償洛基剪掉的西芙金髮，伊瓦爾迪之子矮人鍛出金髮、指環德羅普尼爾與神船斯基德布拉德尼爾；洛基隨即以自己的頭顱打賭，說矮人兄弟布洛克與埃特里鍛不出更好的寶物。在鍛爐旁，一隻蒼蠅——喬裝的洛基——蜇刺鍛工的手與頸以毀其工；第三次時蒼蠅蜇其眼瞼，血流不止，埃特里仍抽出短柄的雷錘妙爾尼爾。諸神裁定雷錘為至寶——可縮小藏於衣內、出手必中、擲出必回——矮人便要斬洛基之頭，而諸神以「頸非頭」的縫線詭計保下其性命。此記錄是雷神標誌性兵器的起源故事，也是矮人贈禮經濟的呈現。

texts.canonical_translation: A. G. Brodeur, Snorri Sturluson: The Prose Edda, New York 1916 (public domain)

narrative.en:
Skaldskaparmal's treasure-chapter is one of the myth-world's wittiest industrial narratives. Loki has cut off all of Sif's hair in malice; Thor seizes him; and the price of the neck is a commission: the dwarf sons of Ivaldi will forge hair of real gold that grows like living hair, and, carried away, also the ship Skidbladnir, which always finds fair wind, and the ring Draupnir, which drops eight rings of itself every ninth night. Loki, wanting to win more, goes to the brothers Brokkr and Eitri and stakes his head that they cannot forge better treasures.

The forge-scene is a contest of endurance. Eitri sets a pigskin in the forge and bids Brokkr blow, 'and not stop until he has taken out of the forge what he had put there'; a fly comes and stings Brokkr's arm, and he blows on regardless; what comes out is the boar Gullinbursti with golden bristles. Then gold goes into the forge, and the fly stings Brokkr's neck, twice as hard, and he blows on; out comes the ring Draupnir. Then iron, and the fly - Loki in the shape of a gadfly - stings Brokkr's eyelid, and when the blood runs down into his eye and he cannot see, he drops the bellows for a moment 'just to brush the fly away' - and what comes out of the forge is the hammer Mjollnir, whose one flaw is the short handle.

The judgment at Asgard formalizes the myth's doctrine. Odin rules: the hammer is the best of all treasures - 'for it is small and can be hidden in the shirt, and it never misses its mark, and it returns to the hand that throws it' - and the sun withers and rock splits at its stroke. Brokkr moves to collect the stake: the head of Loki. Loki consents - to the head - but the dwarf may take no more than the head: so Loki says his neck belongs to him, and the dwarf, denied the knife-path, sews up Loki's lips instead. The gods' economy thus runs on technical theft, wagers and loophole law - and the thunder-god's weapon is forged with a wound in its maker's eye, which is why the world's most reliable weapon has one flaw.

The cultural functions are the divine toolkit's genealogy and the doctrine of flaws. Each god's signature object (Sif's hair, Draupnir, the ship, the boar, the hammer) is a dwarf-gift with a story, and the kenning-system cites them; Mjollnir's short handle is the myth-world's admission that even perfect weapons are accidents of interrupted labor. And Loki's role - the saboteur whose sabotage produces the world's best weapon - is the trickster as quality-control: the fly in the forge is the reason the hammer has a handle too short to be perfect and too true to fail.

In the atlas, the record anchors the forge-gift family (the Greek Hephaestus' works, the Chinese Gan-Jiang and Mo-Ye swords): each a divine weapon with a maker's wound; the Norse one is distinctive in being won by a wager between two dwarf-brother workshops.

functions: Aition of Mjollnir's form: short handle from a saboteur's interruption of the smith
Doctrine of flaws: the world's best weapon is an accident of interrupted labor
Dwarf-gift economy: each god's signature object cited by the kenning-system
Trickster as quality-control: Loki's sabotage produces the best treasure

title.en: Thrymskvida: Thor Dressed as a Bride
title.zh: 《特呂姆之歌》：扮作新娘的索爾

region.en: Thrym's hall in Jotunheim (symbolic pin at Jotunheimen, Norway)
region.zh: 約頓海姆特呂姆之廳（象徵性定位於挪威尤通黑門山）

texts.period: Thrymskvida c. 900-1000 CE; principal MS Codex Regius GKS 2365 4to; also preserved in the Edda MS

source.work: Thrymskvida (complete poem); critical ed. Ursula Dronke (Poetic Edda II, 1997)

texts.license: Public domain (Bellows 1923); passages below are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: The giant Thrym has stolen Thor's hammer and will return it only for Freyja as his bride. Freyja's rage breaks the hall's floors; Heimdall proposes the counter-disguise: Thor dressed as the bride, Loki as the maid of honor. The wedding proceeds against accumulating comedy - Thor eats an ox and eight salmon (the bride eats? the maid explains: eight nights' fasting), drinks three casks, glares when Thrym lifts the veil to kiss her - and at the crucial moment the hammer is laid in the bride's lap to hallow the wedding by Thor's rite; Thor seizes it, kills the groom, the bride's kin and the old sister who begged a gift. The record is the myth's greatest comedy and its doctrine of ritual disguise: the most masculine god saves the world dressed as a woman, because marriage rites are society's most hallowed border.
summary.zh: 巨人特呂姆偷走了索爾的雷錘，並宣稱只有將芙蕾雅許配為妻才會歸還。芙蕾雅的怒火震裂了大廳的地板；海姆達爾獻計反喬裝：索爾扮作新娘，洛基扮作伴娘。婚禮在笑料不斷中推進——新娘一口吃下一頭牛、八條鮭魚（伴娘解釋：八日未進食），豪飲三桶蜜酒，特呂姆掀起面紗欲吻時，新娘眼中雷光如電——而在關鍵時刻，雷錘被放在新娘膝上，以索爾之禮為婚禮祝聖；索爾一把抓住錘柄，擊殺新郎、新娘親族與那位乞求禮物的老姐妹。此記錄是神話中最偉大的喜劇，亦是「儀式喬裝」的教義：最陽剛之神以女裝救世，因為婚禮正是社會最神聖的邊界。

texts.canonical_translation: Henry A. Bellows, The Poetic Edda, New York 1923 (public domain)

narrative.en:
Thrymskvida is the myth corpus's comedy of cross-dressing, and it is also one of its tightest plot-engines. The theft: Thor wakes to find his hammer gone; Loki borrows Freyja's feather-dress, flies to Jotunheim, and Thrym tells him plainly: the hammer lies eight leagues under the earth, 'and no one shall bring it back to Thor unless he bring me Freyja for a wife'. The ransom rejected: Freyja's fury is the poem's great scene - 'then burst Freyja's wrath, and she threw the necklace Brisings from her, so that the floors of the halls trembled, and the great Brising-necklace broke'; no god or goddess will go disguised as her.

The plan and its costume: Heimdall, 'wisest of gods', proposes that Thor go as the bride, with the necklace, keys, woman's clothes, and head-dress; Loki as the maid-servant. Thor's objection - 'the Aesir will call me unmanly if I go as a bride' - is answered by Loki with the poem's logic: 'be silent, Thor, unless the giants settle in the gods' courts'. The costume is completed with a grinding stone? - a millstone under the bridal veil, for shoulders (the poem: 'his eyes burned fiercely? ' - the stone was laid under his woman's-garment, 'and he had a look of rage').

The wedding's comedy is the doctrine. The bridal party arrives at Thrym's hall; the feast begins; the bride eats at evening one ox, eight salmon, all the dainties for women, and drinks three casks of mead - Thrym marvels ('I never saw a bride bite harder, nor a maiden drink more mead'), and the maid's explanation - 'eight nights before coming here, Freyja ate nothing, so eager was she for the wedding' - is the ritual lie that feeds the disguise. Thrym lifts the veil to kiss the bride and leaps back the length of the hall: fire burns in the bride's eyes. The maid explains: she has not slept for eight nights, so hot is her longing for the wedding. Then the sister of the giant begs gifts - 'bring rings of red gold to thy sister' - and Thrym orders the hammer brought in to hallow the bride 'by Thor's rite': 'lay the hammer in the maiden's lap, and hallow us both by the hand of Var'. At that word the thunder-god laughs in his heart? - the poem: 'the heart laughed in Thor's breast when the hard-hearted one knew the hammer', he seizes it first and kills Thrym, then the whole giant-kin, and the old sister who had asked for rings 'she? ' - the poem: he struck her also who begged the wedding-gift, 'and got a blow instead of coin'.

The cultural functions are the ritual-disguise doctrine and the border-theology of marriage. The myth locates society's holiest transaction - marriage, with its ring, veil, feast and bride-price - on the frontier with the giants, and shows that the frontier can be crossed by the gender-disguise of the strongest god: the marriage rite is so hallowed that even a god must enter it in costume. And the poem's Var-doctrine (the goddess of betrothal vows) means the wedding is legally binding: Thrym's hall is a lawful wedding-feast, and the bride's weapon is lawful too. Its reception: the poem is the myth corpus's most parodied and performed text (17th-20th-century ballads, Wagner, Marvel), and its comedy's core - the god of thunder in a bridal veil - has never stopped working.

For the atlas, the record anchors the ritual-disguise family (the Greek Achilles on Skyros, the Chinese Mulan cycle, the Irish Cuchulainn's compulsion into womanhood): each a hero in women's clothes; only the Norse one saves the world by it.

functions: Ritual-disguise doctrine: the marriage rite as society's holiest, most crossable border
Gender-comedy as theology: the most masculine god saves the world in a bridal veil
Legal frame: the wedding under Var's vow makes the feast lawful - and the weapon lawful
The myth's greatest comedy: plotted theft, angry goddess, wedding sabotage

title.en: Thor and Hrungnir: The Duel with the Stone Giant
title.zh: 索爾大戰石巨人赫朗格尼爾

region.en: Griots? - the duel-plain at Jotunheimr (symbolic pin at Jotunheimen, Norway)
region.zh: 決戰平原，約頓海姆（象徵性定位於挪威尤通黑門山）

texts.period: Skaldskaparmal c. 1220-1230 (older material); Haustlong (Thjodolfr of Hvinir, c. 900); principal MSS Codex Regius GKS 2367 4to

source.work: Snorri, Skaldskaparmal ch. 9 (Thor and Hrungnir); Thjodolfr of Hvinir, Haustlong; ed. Vigfusson & Powell, CPB 1883

texts.license: Public domain (Brodeur 1916; CPB 1883); passages below are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: The giant Hrungnir, drunk on Odin's mead, boasts he will carry Valhalla off to Jotunheim and drink all the Aesir's ale; cornered at Griots? - at the duel-ground, he faces Thor with a whetstone and a heart of stone. Thor's hammer meets the whetstone in the air; the stone shatters, one splinter sticks in Thor's head, and the hammer crushes the giant's stone skull. The fallen giant's leg pins Thor until his three-year-old son Magni heaves it off; a sorceress' clay giant, Mokkurkalfi, melts in terror at the thunder-god's approach. The duel leaves Thor with a whetstone in his skull and the aition of the quern-hone in every valley: Hrungnir's shattered stone is why the landscape is full of the giant's broken weapons.
summary.zh: 巨人赫朗格尼爾在奧丁處醉飲後誇口，要將瓦爾哈拉整座搬到約頓海姆，喝盡阿薩神族的美酒；被迫應戰的他在決戰平原上以磨石為盾、以石為心面對索爾。雷錘在空中與磨石相撞，磨石碎裂，一片碎石嵌進索爾頭顱，雷錘則擊碎巨人的石頭腦袋。倒下的巨人以其腿壓住索爾，直至三歲的兒子曼尼將其掀開；女巫所製的黏土巨人莫庫卡爾菲在雷神逼近時嚇得融化。這場決鬥讓索爾頭中留下一枚磨石碎片，也解釋了為何山谷間遍布碎裂的磨石——那正是巨人被打碎的兵器。

texts.canonical_translation: A. G. Brodeur, Snorri Sturluson: The Prose Edda, New York 1916 (public domain); Haustlong via Corpus Poeticum Boreale 1883

narrative.en:
The duel begins as a guest's impertinence. Hrungnir, the strongest of giants, is invited into Asgard as Odin's guest, drinks himself mad on the god's mead, and boasts: he will carry off Valhalla to Jotunheim, empty the Aesir's ale-cellar, and carry off Freyja and Sif for his housewives. The gods call Thor from the east; Hrungnir, armed in stone - 'his head and heart were of stone, hard as any rock' - demands single combat at the frontier, 'for it would have been a disgrace if Thor had come upon him unprepared'.

The duel is myth's staged physics. The giants, fearing the result, make a clay man nine leagues tall - Mokkurkalfi ('mist-calf'), with a mare's heart, which trembles so at Thor's thunder that it wets itself and hides. Hrungnir stands with his whetstone raised; Thor casts the hammer; the whetstone and the hammer meet in the air, and the stone breaks - 'part fell to the earth, whence come all flint-rocks? ' - Snorri's aition: the shards of Hrungnir's whetstone are the world's flint. One splinter sticks in Thor's head; the hammer strikes the giant's stone skull and shatters it; and as Hrungnir falls, 'his leg came over Thor's neck, and he was pinned'. All the giants could not lift the leg; Thor's son Magni, three winters old, lifts it, saying: 'had I been older, I would have shaken the giant off with my fist' - the earliest exploit of the god who will inherit the hammer.

The wound's sequel is the myth's medical-ritual coda: the sorceress Groa, wife of the rune-wight Aurvandil, comes to sing healing-charms over Thor's head, and the whetstone begins to loosen; Thor, delighted, tells her that her husband is alive - carried homeward in a basket from Jotunheim, one toe frozen and knocked off into the sky to be a star (Aurvandil's Toe) - and at the good news Groa forgets her charms, 'so that the whetstone never came out'. Thor's headache is permanent: the fragment is why thunder-god statues? - the doctrine: the stone in the head is the myth's explanation of the god's essential vulnerability, and Groa's interrupted charm is the aition of half-cured wounds.

The skaldic evidence: Thjodolfr of Hvinir's Haustlong (c. 900), a shield-poem, narrates the duel in kennings - 'the stony-hearted one' whose skull the hammer broke - centuries before Snorri, evidencing the myth's court currency. And the cultural functions: the duel formalizes the god-giant warfare as single combat at the frontier; the whetstone-in-the-head is the aition of flint and of the god's wound; and Mokkurkalfi's mare-heart is the myth's satire of manufactured armies. In the atlas, the duel answers the Greek Heracles-Geryon combats and the Chinese Yi's archery duels: each a frontier single-combat with geological aftermath.

functions: Aition of flint: Hrungnir's shattered whetstone as the world's flint-rocks
Doctrine of the god's wound: the whetstone in Thor's skull, permanently half-cured
Frontier single-combat: god-giant warfare formalized as a duel at the border
Skaldic documentation: Haustlong (c. 900) evidences the myth centuries before Snorri

title.en: Thor's Fishing: The Ox-Head Bait and the World-Serpent's Eye
title.zh: 索爾垂釣：牛頭為餌與世界之蛇之眼

region.en: The deep sea beyond the giant's coasts (symbolic pin at Lofoten, Norway)
region.zh: 巨人海岸之外的深海（象徵性定位於挪威羅弗敦）

texts.license: Public domain (Bellows 1923; CPB 1883; Brodeur 1916); passages below are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: The best-attested exploit in Norse skaldic art: Thor rows out with the giant Hymir, baits the hook with the head of Hymir's best ox, and fishes the World-Serpent off the bottom of the sea. The serpent's head comes over the gunwale, venom dripping, eyes glaring; Thor reaches for the hammer to kill it, and the terrified giant cuts the line; the serpent sinks, struck once on the crown. Snorri adds the doctrine: it is from that blow that the serpent's mark? - no, the monster still lives with the scar, and Thor's fury has its reason: the fishing is the rehearsal of Ragnarok's final duel. Skaldic verse from the 9th century (Bragi, Eysteinn) documents the scene on shields and in lausavisur centuries before the Edda poems.
summary.zh: 這是北歐吟遊詩歌中記載最完備的神蹟：索爾與巨人希米爾出海，以希米爾最好的牛頭為餌，自海底釣起世界之蛇。蛇頭越過船舷，毒液滴落，雙眼圓睜；索爾伸手取錘欲誅之，嚇壞的巨人卻割斷了釣線；巨蛇沉入海底，頭頂留下的一道傷痕。斯諾里補充：此傷至今未癒，怪物仍活著——這一釣正是諸神黃昏最終決戰的預演。早在《埃達》詩歌成文數世紀之前，9世紀的吟遊詩（布拉基的《拉格納之盾》、艾斯泰因的獨立詩句）便已在盾面上記載了這一場景。

texts.canonical_translation: Henry A. Bellows, The Poetic Edda, New York 1923 (public domain); skaldic texts via Corpus Poeticum Boreale 1883

narrative.en:
The fishing-myth is the myth corpus's best-attested narrative, because it lives in three media at once: eddic verse, skaldic shield-poetry and prose doctrine. The eddic version (Hymiskvida) sets the trip inside the kettle-quest: to test the god's appetite, the giant Hymir rows out with the ox-head bait to his deep-sea fishing grounds, 'where he was wont to sit and angle for halibut'; Thor rows on 'past the giants' lands' to the deeps where the serpent lies. The bite is cosmic: 'the line goes taut, the boat heaves? ' - the poem: 'the hook caught the monster, the girdle of all lands below' - and Thor's pull is such that his feet go through the boat's boards to the sea-bottom. The serpent's head comes up over the gunwale 'with venom dripping from its jaws'; Thor reaches for the hammer to kill it - and Hymir, 'pale with terror, cut the line', and the serpent sank away with a blow on its head.

The skaldic attestations are the myth's oldest witnesses. Bragi Boddason's Ragnarsdrapa (9th c.), a shield-poem for Ragnar Lodbrok, describes a shield-picture of the fishing: Thor 'angry? ' - the verses: 'the enemy of the Midgard-serpent'? - Bragi's kennings name the god as 'the tester of the serpent's jaw? ' and the giant's line-cut; and Eysteinn Valdason's lausavisur (10th c.) devote three stanzas to the scene: 'the splendid god? with the ox-head's hook lifted the girdle of the earth'. The images on actual Viking-age stones and cross-slabs (Altuna stone, Gosforth) show the scene carved - the myth documented in four media, which makes it the corpus's strongest case for a pan-Scandinavian mythic iconography.

Snorri's doctrine adds the eschatological freight: the blow Thor struck the serpent's crown is the wound that does not heal, and at Ragnarok the two will meet again - Thor's fishing is the rehearsal of his death-duel, when the tail releases and the venom comes. The ox-head bait is the myth's economy of the frontier: the god fishes with the giant's own property (the ox of the giant's herd, killed at the giant's table), so the exploit is theft upon theft - the kettle, the fish, the ox - all hauled from the borderlands to feed the gods' feast.

Cultural functions: the sea as the serpent's body (the world's girdle, hooked from below); the fishing as rehearsal of doom (the wound that never closes); and the four-media documentation (eddic, skaldic, iconographic, prose) that makes this the myth corpus's strongest cross-media record. In the atlas, the fishing answers the Chinese Nezha's sea-battles and the Greek Heracles' Triton episodes: each a hero versus the sea's monster; only the Norse one is an angling contest with the world's edge.

functions: Sea-as-serpent doctrine: the world's girdle hooked from below
Rehearsal of Ragnarok: the unhealed wound schedules the final duel
Frontier economy: the exploit is theft upon theft (ox, fish, kettle) from the giants
Four-media documentation: eddic, skaldic, iconographic, prose - the corpus's strongest cross-media record

title.en: Thor and Geirrod: The Thorsdrapa and the Brokendown River
title.zh: 索爾大戰蓋爾羅德：《索爾頌》與碎裂之河

region.en: Geirrod's hall across the Vimur river (symbolic pin at Jotunheimen, Norway)
region.zh: 維穆爾河對岸的蓋爾羅德之廳（象徵性定位於挪威尤通黑門山）

texts.period: Thorsdrapa (Eilifr Godrunarson, c. 10th c.); Skaldskaparmal c. 1220-1230; principal MSS Codex Regius GKS 2367 4to

source.work: Eilifr Godrunarson, Thorsdrapa; Snorri, Skaldskaparmal ch. 10 (the story of Thorsdrapa); ed. Vigfusson & Powell, CPB 1883

texts.license: Public domain (CPB 1883; Brodeur 1916); passages below are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: The most violent exploit in skaldic art: Loki, forced by Geirrod's capture of him, decoys Thor into the giant's land without hammer, belt or gloves; the giantess Grid lends the god her belt of strength, iron gloves and staff. At the Vimur river - swollen by the witch's incantations - Thor wades with the staff, 'and they say that the river rose highest at his shoulders', and he finds a stone and hurls it: 'and that stone stayed the stream, as if a rock had been set there' - the aition of a boulder-stopped river. In the hall, Geirrod's iron-hot wedge? - the giant hurls a molten iron wedge with tongs; Thor catches it in his iron gloves and hurls it back through pillar and giant. The skaldic Thorsdrapa, the corpus's most violent poem, tells the same with blood-drinking kennings.
summary.zh: 這是吟遊詩歌中最暴烈的神蹟：洛基被蓋爾羅德擒獲後受迫誘騙索爾——不帶錘、不帶腰帶與鐵手套——深入巨人之地；女巨人格里德借予雷神神力腰帶、鐵手套與木杖。在維穆爾河畔——河水因女巫咒語而暴漲——索爾執杖涉水，「據說河水最高漲至他的肩頭」；他拾起一塊巨石擲出：「那石頭便攔住了水流，如同天然巨岩立於河中」——這是巨石攔河的起源故事。在廳中，巨人以鐵鉗擲出熾熱的鐵楔；索爾以鐵手套接住，反擲回去，貫穿石柱與巨人。吟遊詩《索爾頌》——歌謠中最暴烈的作品——以嗜血的隱喻講述同一故事。

texts.canonical_translation: Corpus Poeticum Boreale, ed. Vigfusson & Powell, Oxford 1883 (public domain); Skaldskaparmal via Brodeur 1916

narrative.en:
The tale's frame is a deception within a deception. Geirrod the giant captures Loki (in hawk-shape) and releases him only on his oath to bring Thor to the hall without his hammer or his strength-girdle; Loki decoys the god with a lying tale of hospitality. The journey is armed by a third party: the giantess Grid, mother of Vidar, warns Thor and lends him her belt of strength, her iron gloves and her staff Gridarvolr.

The river-crossing is the poem's physics-set-piece. The witch Gjalp, Geirrod's daughter, stands astride the Vimur and raises the water with incantations; Thor wades with the staff, 'and they say that the river rose highest at his shoulders'; he finds a stone in the riverbed and casts it, 'and that stone stayed the stream, as if a rock had been set there' - Snorri's aition for a river dammed by a thrown boulder - and then he wades out and grips a mountain-berry? - the prose: he seizes a rowan-tree (the famous 'Thor's salvation' of the rowan) and climbs out; whence the kenning that the rowan is 'Thor's salvation'. In the hall, the tests turn physical: Gjalp, hidden under Thor's chair, presses it up with her knees; the god breaks her back by seating himself hard. Geirrod, seeing the god's fury, hurls a wedge of molten iron with tongs; Thor catches it in the iron gloves and hurls it back 'so that it passed through the pillar and through Geirrod and through the wall, and so out? ' - and the giant's daughters, fleeing, are crushed.

The skaldic poem Thorsdrapa by Eilifr Godrunarson (10th c.) is the myth's oldest and most violent telling - so violent that the Edda-MSS preserve it 'because it is hard to understand? ' - Snorri says he quotes it 'because it is excellent and? ' - the prose says he includes it for its art. The poem's kennings drink blood: Geirrod's hall is 'the wolf-feeding hall? ', the wedge 'the reddening? iron of the giant', Thor 'the breaker of Geirrod's brain-pan'. Snorri retells it to explain the poem's obscure diction - the prose retelling exists for the verse, a case-study of the myth corpus's transmission: skaldic difficulty generating prose narrative.

The record's cultural functions are the river-as-attack doctrine (the frontier's waters weaponized by witchcraft, dammed by a god) and the counter-throw doctrine (the god defeats the giant's technology with the giant's own weapon, caught and returned). And the rowan-tree doctrine ('Thor's salvation') is an aition of folk botanical belief - the rowan's protective reputation in Scandinavian farm-culture descends from this river-crossing. In the atlas, the record anchors the duel-by-technology family: the Chinese Yi's archery, the Greek Heracles' poisoning? - no: the atlas frame is the hero armed by borrowed gear (Grid's belt answers the Greek Athena's aegis-loans), and the myth's weapons are industrial: molten iron against iron gloves.

functions: River-as-attack doctrine: frontier waters weaponized by witchcraft, dammed by a thrown boulder
Counter-throw doctrine: the giant's molten iron caught in iron gloves and returned
Aition of the rowan: 'Thor's salvation' as the tree's protective reputation in farm-culture
Transmission case-study: a violent skaldic poem generating its own prose retelling
